Since 2004, Martinis has served on the faculty of the University of California, Santa Barbara. He held the title of Susan and Bruce Worster Chair in Experimental Physics for many years. The quantum device he developed in collaboration with UCSB colleagues was named Science magazine's 2010 Breakthrough of the Year. Google Quantum AI Lab, a partnership between UC Santa Barbara and Google, announced in 2014 that it had hired Martinis and his team in a multimillion dollar deal to build a quantum computer using superconducting qubits. He and his team published a paper in Nature in 2019, where they presented how they achieved quantum supremacy for the first time using the Sycamore processor, a 53-qubit quantum processor. Martinis resigned from Google in April 2020 after being reassigned to an advisory role.
In 2020, Martinis joined Silicon Quantum Computing, a start-up founded in Australia by Professor Michelle Simmons.
In 2026, he was appointed to the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST) by President Donald Trump."}, {"source": "John M. His father, a Croat from Komiža on the island of Vis near Split, Croatia, immigrated to the United States from Yugoslavia to escape the communist regime. His mother was born in San Pedro to parents who had also emigrated from Croatia.
Martinis studied physics at the University of California, Berkeley, where he received a Bachelor of Science in 1980 and a Doctor of Philosophy in 1987.
During his doctoral studies, Martinis investigated the quantum behaviour of a macroscopic variable, the phase difference across a Josephson tunnel junction. His doctoral advisor was John Clarke. During this time, he collaborated with Michel Devoret, a postdoctoral researcher at the time.
In 1985, Clarke, Devoret, and Martinis presented their analysis of microwave pulses that demonstrated the quantized energy levels of a Josephson junction. This work would later become the basis for superconducting quantum computing.
On September 21, 2026, the Prime Minister of Croatia, Andrej Plenković, granted Martinis Croatian citizenship."}]

content.text:
The 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics went to John Clarke, Michel Devoret and John M. Martinis. The prize was "for the discovery of macroscopic quantum mechanical tunnelling and energy quantisation in an electric circuit" [2025 Nobel Prizes > Prizes; List of Nobel laureates in Physics > Laureates].

Their university affiliations:
- **John Clarke:** University of California, Berkeley, where he is Professor Emeritus [people_search].
- **Michel Devoret:** University of California, Santa Barbara, where he is Professor of Physics. He is also Professor Emeritus of Applied Physics at Yale University and Chief Scientist for Quantum Hardware at Google Quantum AI [people_search].
- **John M. Martinis:** University of California, Santa Barbara, where he is Professor of Physics and has been on the faculty since 2004 [John M. Martinis > Introduction; John M. Martinis > Career]. The people directory had no record for him, so this comes from Wikipedia. The same source says he joined the start-up Silicon Quantum Computing in 2020, but it doesn't say whether he still holds that role. His degrees (B.S. 1980, Ph.D. 1987) are from UC Berkeley, where Clarke was his doctoral advisor [John M. Martinis > Early life and education].

Schoelkopf at Yale University and Université de Sherbrooke in 2007. Its name is an abbreviation of the term transmission line shunted plasma oscillation qubit; one which consists of a Cooper-pair box \"where the two superconductors are also [capacitively] shunted in order to decrease the sensitivity to charge noise, while maintaining a sufficient anharmonicity for selective qubit control\".\nThe transmon achieves its reduced sensitivity to charge noise by significantly increasing the ratio of the Josephson energy to the charging energy. This is accomplished through the use of a large shunting capacitor. The result is energy level spacings that are approximately independent of offset charge. Planar on-chip transmon qubits have T 1 coherence times approximately 30 μs to 40 μs. Recent work has shown significantly improved T 1 times as long as 95 μs by replacing the superconducting transmission line cavity with a three-dimensional superconducting cavity, and by replacing niobium with tantalum in the transmon device, T 1 is further improved up to 0.3 ms. content.text:
A transmon is a type of superconducting charge qubit used in superconducting quantum computing. It is designed to be less sensitive to charge noise [Transmon > Introduction].

- **Name:** "Transmon" is short for "transmission line shunted plasma oscillation qubit" [Transmon > Introduction].
- **Design:** It is a Cooper-pair box whose two superconductors are also capacitively shunted. This reduces sensitivity to charge noise and keeps enough anharmonicity for selective qubit control [Transmon > Introduction].
- **How it works:** A large shunting capacitor raises the ratio of Josephson energy to charging energy. As a result, the energy level spacings are approximately independent of offset charge [Transmon > Introduction].
- **Origin:** Researchers at Yale University and Université de Sherbrooke developed it in 2007. They included Jens Koch, Terri Yu, Jay Gambetta, Andrew Houck, David Schuster, Johannes Majer, Alexandre Blais, Michel Devoret, Steven Girvin and Robert Schoelkopf [Transmon > Introduction].
- **Coherence:** Planar on-chip transmons have T1 coherence times of about 30–40 μs. A 3D superconducting cavity has given T1 times up to 95 μs. Replacing niobium with tantalum has raised T1 to as much as 0.3 ms [Transmon > Introduction].
- **Use:** Transmons are the default qubit in most large-scale quantum processors. Google's Willow chip has 105 physical transmon qubits, and IBM, Rigetti and IQM also use them [Transmon > Superconducting quantum processors]. They also serve as ancillas to control the bosonic modes of a cavity in bosonic-code error correction [Transmon > Bosonic or hybrid quantum memory].

The search results don't link the transmon to any Nobel Prize, so I can't say anything about that from these sources.

content.text:
According to the Wikipedia list of physics laureates, the Nobel Prize in Physics has been awarded to **230 individuals as of 2026** [List of Nobel laureates in Physics > Statistics].

- **Repeat winner:** John Bardeen won twice, in 1956 and 1972 [List of Nobel laureates in Physics > Statistics]. The source gives the total as individuals, so I take it to count him once, but it doesn't say so outright.
- **Latest entries:** The laureate table lists John Clarke, Michel Devoret and John M. Martinis for 2025. It also has a 2026 row for Francis Halzen, "for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin" [List of Nobel laureates in Physics > Laureates]. I didn't check the 2026 entry against any other source.
